So we have had a few negative interactions with patients and their families in the last shift.

So the first is to adjust your style of communication. This includes keeping a calm

So today we are going to talk about quite a daunting topic, explaining immunisations to
parents. Before I get started, I want to preface this session by saying that it's going to be a
quick overview of a general counselling situation. You will likely find yourself saying, but how could
I possibly get through all of this in one visit? And the answer is you wouldn't be expected to.
but it is better to be prepared to cover several different areas related to the central theme of immunisation in case they arise.
These areas include explaining what immunisations are and why we do them,
explaining the needs and benefits of immunisations,
the process of getting immunised as well as public perceptions of immunisations, such as the MMR scandal.
So once you have established the reasons for a patient's visit to the clinic,
you can ask the parent or carer what they already know about the vaccination programme
and just as important what they want to know. Parents may have particular concerns regarding
the vaccination programme and being open to hearing these concerns is the best approach.
Dismissing people's concerns will only lead to frustration all round. When you are explaining
to patients' parents what immunisations are and why we do them, you should emphasise that the
vaccination programme is very safe and that almost all babies have them. This segues into the idea
of herd immunity and that by stopping the disease from developing in one child, we also stop that
child from spreading the disease. Another topic here are the short and long-term effects to a
child of catching an extremely harmful disease. As you're explaining, be sure to frequently check
for understanding by asking if everything is making sense or if they have any questions.
Parents may also want to know about routine vaccinations,
so it's important to have some understanding of each vaccine and the disease it prevents.
However, it's also important not to bombard parents with lots of technical information
and instead to highlight the key benefits.
Routine vaccines that you should be familiar with include
bordetella, pertussis, diphtheria, haemophilius, influenza B, HPV, measles, mumps, pneumococcus,
polio, rotavirus, rubella and tetanus. For each vaccine you should know key facts such as if the
vaccine is live versus toxin, symptoms of the illness, complications, incubation period as well
as how the disease is transmitted and populations particularly affected by the disease.
Once you've gone through specific vaccines that the parent or carer wants to know about
you can also explain to them what to expect on vaccine day
as this will help them to feel more relaxed about the experience as a whole
You should start off by saying that the practitioner will give the injection after screening for contraindications
which is done by asking about how the patient has been doing lately
whether the patient has started on any new medication
had any new diagnoses or any allergic reactions
It's also necessary to explain normal reactions such as crying, irritability and low fever
as well as measures that the carer can take like ensuring the child keeps up their fluids
Finally you need to cover the more extreme reactions that can occur
such as rashes and swelling
but this should be done with information about how rare they are
Another topic that may come up during the consultation is MMR and its link to autism
Our advice here is to explain the study that gave rise to this information and then the new evidence
that has come to light since without going into too many specifics unless there are specific
questions. You might say that there was a piece of research published a number of years ago
claiming a link between MMR and autism. However, since its release, it has been discredited.
The research was on a very small group of individuals and the outcomes were biased by several factors
At the end of the consultation it is recommended that you summarise the topics covered
including which vaccinations the parent is consenting to at this time
It is also strongly recommended to check parental or carer understanding
to make sure there has been no miscommunication
You can also provide parents with an information leaflet on the relevant vaccinations and discuss the scheduling of other vaccinations.

So I have here today Dr Laura Sanders, a researcher interested in slowing Alzheimer's progression.
So, Dr Laura, is it fair to call you a comeback kid?
Hmm, I don't know if anyone should call me a kid.
And as for the comeback part, it isn't me that made a comeback so much.
And it isn't me that made a comeback so much as it is the interest in this drug and its potential to slow the progression of Alzheimer's.
So for our listeners who haven't heard about this drug and its history, can you please give us some background?
Of course. So the drug was shelved early last year by the companies developing it for what appeared to be lacklustre preliminary results.
However, a more in-depth look at the data as well as the incorporation of more data from two clinical trials
suggested that patients on the largest doses of the drug, aducanumab, did indeed benefit.
Can you give us a bit more information about these clinical trials?
Well, as I said, there were two clinical trials done at various sites around the world,
including the US, Canada, Australia, as well as several European and Asian countries.
Both were 18 months in length and randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 studies
which are conducted to confirm and expand on safety and effectiveness results from early studies
done to compare the drug to standard therapies as well as to evaluate the overall risks and benefits of it.
As for the population of the study, it included people with early Alzheimer's disease.
So what you're saying is that quite a bit of time and effort had already been put into this drug when it was shelved.
Yes, that's right, and money of course on the part of the company developing this drug.
But with any drug or treatment, years and years of research and trials are done before the public ever hears about it.
So what was found exactly when the data was re-examined?
Well, people who took the highest amounts of the drug were found to have declined 30% less
as measured by a commonly used Alzheimer's scale than people who took a placebo.
These results have reignited research into the drug.
So, speaking of the drug aducanumab, how does it work?
The drug is an antibody designed to target clusters of amyloid,
which is a sticky protein that is believed to accumulate in the brains of people with Alzheimer's.
I say believed because there are still some researchers that argue that the presence of amyloid is a red herring.
But research on this drug showing that clearing the amyloid slows the decline of patients is further evidence of the significance of the presence of amyloid.
Brain scans of patients who received the drug also showed less tau, another protein associated with Alzheimer's.
No matter what ends up happening with this drug,
it has definitely provided new evidence about the role of different proteins in the development of Alzheimer's.
And what about side effects?
Is it true that doses were initially kept low in the clinical trials because of concern about possible side effects?
Yes, that is true.
And as with any drug, there are some side effects.
So around 40% of people who received the highest dose of aducanumab
showed signs of brain swelling or bleeding according to scans.
But most didn't go on to exhibit any symptoms of those problems.
So what do you think will be the final verdict on this drug?
Well, I think it's too early to tell just yet.
I mean, I think one key lesson from all of this is that science takes time.
We can't rush it.
I mean, I know there are researchers calling the results exhilarating and an important moment for the Alzheimer's field, and I am also optimistic, but cautiously so.
I mean, there are aspects of this study that complicate matters.
As you mentioned in a previous question, there was a concern about dosing, which resulted in a change in dosing midway through the trial, and then there was the trial's early ends.
Both of these changes further complicate the research and analysis.
Those complexities and the whiplash they have caused have understandably left some researchers wary of these newest results.
Personally, I am withholding judgement until more data is available.
More independent analyses of the drug are needed.
It has been a pleasure.
